seo.title: Karmic tail 12 7 13 compatibility: Koschei on twelve chains
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 7 13 compatibility: The Hanged Man, The Chariot and Death. What a couple keeps on hold, why it keeps running, and how to finish the old.

title: The 12-7-13 karmic tail in couple compatibility: Koschei on twelve chains
short: The Hanged Man, The Chariot, Death. In the deck, cards twelve and thirteen lie side by side, yet in this couple's tail The Chariot has driven in between them. No personal destiny matrix contains this triple: it takes two people to make it. The 12-7-13 karmic tail in compatibility is not about a love that will end. It is about something old that never ended because nobody finished it. It was hung up instead.

paragraphs: "Marya Morevna" is number 159 in Alexander Afanasyev's "Narodnye russkie skazki" (Russian Folk Tales); the quotations below follow W. R. S. Ralston's English translation of 1873, which spells the villain Koshchei. The tale opens with a death. Prince Ivan's parents, as they lie dying, tell their son about his three sisters: "Give your sisters in marriage to the very first suitors who come to woo them. Don't go keeping them by you!" Ivan obeys. A falcon, an eagle and a raven fly in to woo the sisters, and each time the prince answers in the same spirit: "I will not interfere with her liberty of choice." He knows how to let go.

Left alone, he rides out to look for his sisters and finds a plain covered with a slain army. One woman has slain it all: Marya Morevna. Her first words to Ivan are a question: "whither does God send you? and is it of your free will or against your will?" — "Not against their will do brave youths ride!" — "Well, if your business be not pressing, tarry awhile in my tent." Two nights in the tent, and a wedding.

Then the princess goes off to war. She leaves her husband all the housekeeping and a single prohibition: "Go about everywhere, keep watch over everything, only do not venture to look into that closet there." The next sentence in the tale is five words long: "He couldn't help doing so." In the closet "there hung Koshchei the Deathless, fettered by twelve chains". Koschei begs: "Have pity upon me and give me to drink! Ten years long have I been here in torment." Ivan hands him a bucket, a second, a third. After the third Koschei "regained his former strength, gave his chains a shake, and broke all twelve at once" — and carries Marya Morevna off in a whirlwind.

The middle of the tale is a chase. Three times Ivan finds his wife and three times he takes her away. "Remember not the past; much better fly with me while Koshchei the Deathless is out of sight. Perhaps he won't catch us." When Koschei's horse learns of the escape, it answers its master without any hurry: "It is possible to sow wheat, to wait till it grows up, to reap it and thresh it, to grind it to flour, to make five pies of it, to eat those pies, and then to start in pursuit — and even then to be in time." The second time Ivan no longer hopes to get away: "Suppose he does catch us. At all events we shall have spent an hour or two together." The third time: "Let him hew away! I cannot live without you." Koschei chops him into little pieces, puts them in a barrel, smears it with pitch, binds it with iron hoops and flings it into the blue sea.

The brothers-in-law learn of the disaster from the silver Ivan left them as keepsakes: it has turned black. The Eagle drags the barrel ashore, the Falcon flies for the Water of Life, the Raven for the Water of Death. "The Raven sprinkled them with the Water of Death — the pieces joined together, the body became whole. The Falcon sprinkled it with the Water of Life — Prince Ivan shuddered, stood up, and said: 'Ah! what a time I've been sleeping!'"

And now, for the first time, Ivan asks something other than how to escape. He asks his wife to "find out from Koshchei the Deathless whence he got so good a steed". The answer lies beyond the fiery river, with Baba Yaga: Koschei herded her mares for three days and was given a foal for it. Ivan goes to the same place. The mares scatter, he weeps and falls asleep on a stone, and the herd is driven home for him by a bird, a lioness and a bee whose young and whose honey he spared on the way. From the stable he takes "a sorry colt rolling in the muck" and fattens it in the green meadows until "it turned into a wondrous steed".

The last time, Koschei's horse answers differently: "God knows! Prince Ivan has a horse now which is better than I." Koschei says, "Well, I can't stand it," and gives chase. Ivan's horse strikes him with its hoof, and the prince burns Koschei on a pyre and scatters his ashes to the wind. The ending: "Then Marya Morevna mounted Koshchei's horse and Prince Ivan got on his own."

The numbers do not say which partner in a real couple is Ivan and which is Marya Morevna. The tale itself swaps the usual roles: she rides off to war, he keeps the house. In a couple with this tail both roles usually fall to both people in turn: each of them has a closet, and each has at least once given water to someone else's Koschei.

sections.h2: 12 · Entry to the task: the pact of the locked closet
paragraphs: The entry to the task, point M, is what the couple wants together: its shared language and its agreements. With this wish the two enter the task, and the same wish later pushes back. This couple's entry is The Hanged Man: the wish to stop time.

That is exactly how the tale begins. Not "let us marry", but "if your business be not pressing, tarry awhile". A union with the 12-7-13 tail often forms as a breathing space: two people meet at a breaking point, after their own war or someone else's, and the first thing they give each other is a pause. Nobody hurries here, nobody asks too much, everybody is gentle. For two tired people that is a great deal.

Such a pause has a mechanism: a place nobody looks into. For one couple it is a previous marriage about which "everything has been said". For another it is a parent's voice that still decides for both of them when to buy a flat. For a third it is an abandoned career, a debt, a grudge, a promise made to someone before they met. She does not ask why he rings his mother back every evening at nine. He does not ask why the box with her old life has travelled unopened through three house moves. Peace at home rests on Marya Morevna's rule: go everywhere, only do not look in here.

The catch is that what hangs does not die. Koschei hangs for ten years without food or drink, and he is alive. He is Deathless not because he is stronger than death but because he was hung up rather than killed. Everything the couple has put off "for later" is kept whole in the closet, with all its former strength. Twelve turns up in the tale once more: around Baba Yaga's house stand twelve poles, eleven of them with heads, "the twelfth alone remained unoccupied". Both times it is the number of what hangs and waits for its hour.

The resistance of this point sounds like pity. "Have pity upon me and give me to drink" is a request nobody refuses the first time. One bucket is mercy. The second is habit. After the third the old thing "regained his former strength", and the chains break all at once, all twelve. In a couple's life the third bucket looks innocent: bailing out an ex one more time, one last loan to a brother, one more long talk with the person who used to decide for both of them. Among the difficulties of The Hanged Man in a couple, Lisovskaya names pressure on pity and the inability to say no. The tale shows the same thing without any moral: the old does not need freedom, it needs water.

One more detail. The closet opens not by decision but by impatience: "He couldn't help doing so." The pause ends on its own, while the mistress is far away, and only one of them looks inside. What matters for this couple is not whether the door will open (it will) but whether they open it together or one of them opens it alone, in secret.

sections.h2: 7 · Middle of the task: three escapes on a borrowed horse
paragraphs: The middle of the task, point N, shows how the couple travels from the shared wish to the main task: what it does and what it goes through. Here it is The Chariot — motion, drive, a joint leap forward.

As soon as the closet is open, the couple runs. The tale gives the exact formula of escape: "Remember not the past; much better fly with me… Perhaps he won't catch us." The Russian original ends with "avos ne dogonit": avos is the untranslatable Russian "maybe it will work out somehow". Not a conversation about Koschei, but the road. In a real couple this is a move to another city "with a clean slate", a quick wedding, a new business, a long trip after which "everything will settle down". The trip really does help for about two weeks. Then the old argument catches up with the two of them in the new kitchen, word for word.

The Chariot in a couple is not foolishness. Lisovskaya writes about strong passion at the start of such unions and about how the partners rise to defend each other. The tenderest line of the tale is spoken in flight: "At all events we shall have spent an hour or two together." The two really do get those hours. But an escape on an ordinary horse is a date, not a solution. The old has the better horse, and it is in no hurry: it has time to sow wheat, reap it, thresh it, bake it and eat it, "and even then to be in time".

The three escapes end in a barrel in the sea. This is The Chariot's minus: motion that no longer checks itself against the goal, and strength drawn from the people closest instead of gathered on one's own. Koschei, after all, got his strength back from water out of Ivan's hands.

The turning point of the middle is a single question. Once revived, Ivan stops asking how to escape and asks to learn "whence he got so good a steed". It is Marya Morevna who finds out: she "chose a favorable moment" and questioned the one she knows best of all. For a couple this is the shift from running to investigating: what gives the old script its strength, where it gets that strength, who keeps feeding it. The tale's answer is unexpectedly ordinary. Koschei earned his horse: he herded the mares for three days and did not lose one. The old had no magic, only years of service.

Benebell Wen writes that The Chariot can mean a journey "not for the sake of travel, but for the sake of acquisition". The trip to Baba Yaga is exactly that: Ivan goes not to hide but to earn a horse of his own. The prize looks pitiful: "a sorry colt rolling in the muck". It becomes a wondrous steed only after it has been fattened in the meadows. A couple's own strength begins just as unimpressively: the first honest agreement, the first budget without help from the parents, the first trip that nobody needs to escape from. It has to be raised.

sections.h2: 13 · Main task: letting the Deathless die
paragraphs: The main task, point D, is what the couple has to learn and what does not come easily; it is read above all through the difficulty. Here it is Death. And the enemy in the tale is named as its exact opposite: Koschei the Deathless.

The task of the 12-7-13 tail is not to lose something. It is to let something end that cannot end by itself, because it is hanging. In the deck 12 and 13 are neighbours, and the difference between them is the difference between "postpone" and "complete". As long as the old thing hangs, it is deathless.

Death has two faces in this tale, and that is its most important detail. W. R. S. Ralston, who translated the tale into English in 1873, noticed that a magic water which brings the dead back to life appears in the folklore of all lands, but in the Slavonic stories there are "the two waters, each performing one part only" of the work. The Water of Death does not kill: under it "the pieces joined together, the body became whole". The Water of Life wakes. First the water that belongs to death gathers what was cut apart into a whole, and only then does life return.

For the couple this is the main task read in its plus: an ending that gathers. After three escapes the two are left with pieces — things unsaid, grudges, two different versions of one story. The Water of Death is the last conversation after which no further one is needed. Signed papers. An unpacked box. A flat that has finally been sold. Parents who have heard a calm "we have decided for ourselves". This is not drama but assembly. Afterwards a couple will often say Ivan's line: "Ah! what a time I've been sleeping!"

The tale itself opens with death: with the dying parents' instruction, "Don't go keeping them by you!" Among the tasks of Death in a couple, Lisovskaya names helping each other to separate from parents, moves and partings, and the ability to see one's own mistakes and not only the other person's. In the tale all this fits into a single exchange. Marya Morevna: "why did you disobey me…?" Ivan: "Remember not the past." Each looks at the other's part: she at his curiosity, he right past her closet. Yet the closet was shared: it took both her locked door and his pity.

The minus of this point is a Death that one partner imposes on the other. One demands that the other "finally change". In the present partner one looks for the features of a former one. There are so many changes that the other has nothing left to stand on. The plus is a Death that the two go through together. Lisovskaya describes such couples as living proof that life goes on after something hard, and as a union in which each accepts the partner's past and moves on.

The tale shows this plus in its last line. Koschei is burnt, his ashes scattered; nobody can hang him up again. And then "Marya Morevna mounted Koshchei's horse and Prince Ivan got on his own". The past is not erased: its strength has become her horse. Beside her rides the second rider, on a horse he raised himself. Two horses side by side are The Chariot in its plus: riding together, each on a road of their own.

sections.h2: Waite: the rider who is in no hurry
paragraphs: In Arthur Edward Waite's "The Pictorial Key to the Tarot" these three cards are linked more closely than their numbers suggest.

Waite ends his account of The Hanged Man with Death: whoever understands this symbol "will know that after the sacred Mystery of Death there is a glorious Mystery of Resurrection". And he begins his account of Death with The Hanged Man: the suggestion of death he made at the previous card is to be understood mystically, "but this is not the case in the present instance". The two cards that the tail places at opposite ends talk to each other across a page in Waite. The Hanged Man himself, for Waite, "suggests life in suspension, but life and not death". A ready portrait of Koschei in the closet.

Waite's rider of Death "moves slowly" and "carries no visible weapon", yet "king and child and maiden fall before him". A slow, unarmed rider whom nobody outruns: this is Koschei's horse, which has time for both the wheat and the bread. The Chariot is faster, but Death does not win by speed.

The most unexpected link belongs to The Chariot. Waite recalls that Court de Gébelin saw in it "Osiris Triumphing, the conquering sun in spring-time having vanquished the obstacles of winter", and objects: "Osiris rising from the dead is not represented by such obvious symbolism." Plutarch tells the myth of Osiris ("On Isis and Osiris", chapters 13 and 18, in Babbitt's translation). Typhon shuts his brother in a chest, which the conspirators "fastened by nails from the outside and also by using molten lead", and sends it down the river to the sea. Later he "divided it into fourteen parts", and Isis searches for them, "sailing through the swamps in a boat of papyrus". Ivan has his pitch-smeared barrel, the iron hoops, the blue sea and the pieces gathered by his brothers-in-law. Waite was arguing with a reading of the picture, not with the myth. But the argument itself says a lot: The Chariot was once read as the triumph of someone who had been shut in, thrown into the water, cut apart and put together again. In the 12-7-13 tail The Chariot's true triumph is exactly that: it comes after the Water of Death, not instead of it.

One more of Waite's remarks about Death is useful to a couple. Besides natural death he describes another: entrance "while still in this life" into a state that is "a change in the form of consciousness". This is the death the tail is about: what changes is the form of the union, not the people in it.

sections.h2: Wen: three cards of one water
paragraphs: In "Holistic Tarot" Benebell Wen assigns each card to an element. About The Hanged Man, The Chariot and Death she says the same thing: "The element of Water governs this card." In all three, according to Wen, yin energy is dominant. The 12-7-13 tail is made of water alone.

The tale flows with water too. Ralston explains the name Morevna as "daughter of More, (the Sea or any great water)". Koschei asks for a drink. The barrel with Ivan is flung into the blue sea. Baba Yaga's mares hide in the sea and stand "up to their necks in water". Ivan is raised by the Water of Death and the Water of Life. Fire appears in the tale twice: the fiery river that needs a bridge, and the pyre on which Koschei burns. In this story water preserves and restores strength, including to what ought to end. The old ends only in fire. This is our own reading, but it captures the mechanics of the tail exactly: for a couple made entirely of water, the question is not whether to pour water but which water, and for whom.

Wen also has words about water for each card separately. The Chariot upright is water that "flows quickly forward, with great force"; reversed, it is dammed up. Death asks the Seeker to "be fluid like water" and to "let go of the present and move on". To The Hanged Man Wen gives the pun "hang in there" and a question it shares with The Fool: "will the Seeker fall or fly?" Ivan with his three buckets falls. On his own horse he flies: "it flies just like a bird," he tells his wife.

One more of Wen's readings of Death fits the tale literally: it is the card of revolutions, "the waning of power of one authority and the growing, ascending power of a new". For ten years Koschei ruled the house from the closet. The tail asks the couple to change who rules: not the old order, but the two of them.

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers: a tail that only two can make
paragraphs: **No single person can have it.** In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre of the chart. With a main task of 13, an entry of 12 is impossible with any centre. So 12-7-13 exists only as the sum of two people.
**It is rare.** The tail occurs in about one couple in 3,647 (0.027%) and ranks 93rd of the 97 couple tails.

**It is always built from the same two personal tails.** In every such couple one partner has the personal tail 9-12-3 and the other has 3-13-10. This leads to the main discovery. The twelve at the couple's entry is the middle of the first partner's personal tail. The thirteen in the main task is the middle of the second partner's. The seven in the middle is the sum of the two personal middles: 12 + 13 = 25 → 7. The couple's tail is built entirely from two personal middles. Each partner brings into the union what stands halfway along their own road: one brings what hangs, the other brings what demands an ending. The Chariot appears in neither personal tail: only the couple brings it into the tail.

**The personal tails hook together on The Empress.** The tail 9-12-3 ends with a three, the tail 3-13-10 begins with one, and together they form a single chain, 9-12-3-13-10. In that chain The Empress — home and abundance — stands between The Hanged Man and Death. In the couple's tail her place is taken by The Chariot. Our reading: between the pause and the ending the couple gets not a home but a road, and the home comes after the road. That is how the tale goes. Ralston's version stops at "they went off to their own realm"; Afanasyev's Russian adds the formula "zhit'-pozhivat', dobra nazhivat' da medok popivat'" — they lived on, gathering goods and sipping honey (our translation). The honey, incidentally, comes from the very bee whose hive Ivan left alone.

**The atmosphere inside the couple is always Justice.** This follows from the same two tails. With the tail 3-13-10 the personal centre is always 20, Judgement; with 9-12-3 it is always 6, The Lovers. 6 + 20 = 26 → 8. The tale in which this tail lives is a world of exact accounts. Even Koschei keeps count: "this time I will forgive you, in return for your kindness in giving me water to drink. And a second time I will forgive you; but the third time beware!" The bird, the lioness and the bee return exactly what they received. Justice at the centre of the couple, in its plus, is a fair division of tasks: she rides off to war, he keeps the house, and nobody finds it strange. In its minus it is a ledger of grievances, "I gave you three buckets", promises not kept, like the broken "do not look". Among the tasks of Justice in a couple Lisovskaya lists forgiveness. The tale is a reminder that forgiveness with a counter is not yet forgiveness.

**The couple's values are always The Lovers.** The two came here for a choice. In the tale the key question is asked twice: at the beginning and at the threshold of death. Marya Morevna: "is it of your free will or against your will?" Baba Yaga by her poles: "Is it of your own accord, or on compulsion?" Both times Ivan answers in terms of will, not compulsion: "Not against their will do brave youths ride!" and "I have come to earn from you a heroic steed." He gave his sisters away in the same spirit: "I will not interfere with her liberty of choice." The value of this couple is a union without compulsion, including compulsion by one's own past.

sections.h2: How to calculate the 12-7-13 tail: example 19.03.1979 and 04.01.1976
paragraphs: A couple's matrix is calculated point by point: each point of the couple is the sum of the same points in the two personal matrices, reduced to 22.

First partner, 19.03.1979. Day 19, month 3, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 9 = 26 → 8. Main task 19 + 3 + 8 = 30 → 3, centre 19 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 33 → 6. Entry of the tail 3 + 6 = 9, middle 3 + 9 = 12. Personal tail 9-12-3.
Second partner, 04.01.1976. Day 4, month 1, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. Main task 4 + 1 + 5 = 10, centre 4 + 1 + 5 + 10 = 20. Entry 10 + 20 = 30 → 3, middle 10 + 3 = 13. Personal tail 3-13-10.
The couple's centre is 6 + 20 = 26 → 8, Justice. The couple's values for these dates are 6, The Lovers, as in every couple with this tail.

The middle of a couple's tail is not recalculated from its two ends; it is added up from the two personal middles. For 12-7-13 both methods give the same seven: 12 + 13 is both the sum of the ends and the sum of the two personal middles. In shape the tail is built like a personal one, yet no person has it. No other couple tail is made of the numbers 12, 7 and 13.

sections.h2: How a couple goes through the 12-7-13 tail
paragraphs: The tail does not predict events and passes no sentence. It shows where the couple gets stuck and what changes the plot.

ul: **Open the closet together, in daylight.** Do not wait until one of them "couldn't help doing so" while the other is away. Say out loud what is hanging: "this is something we have not settled".
**Give one bucket, not three.** Pity for the past is normal. Pity without a limit gives it back its strength. Help once and say where the help ends.
**Stop running on an ordinary horse.** A move, a wedding, a new project are good in themselves, but they do not replace the conversation about Koschei.
**Ask the old about its strength.** Where did the script get such a horse: who feeds it, what makes it convenient, what holds it up.

**Raise a horse of your own.** One's own strength starts as a sorry colt: small agreements that are kept. Help comes from those the couple did not wrong along the way — people who were treated fairly.
**Give the ending its Water of Death.** Do not tear things off; gather them: the last conversation, the papers, the unpacked boxes. An ending that needs no going back.
**Do not hang it up again.** Burning it and scattering the ashes to the wind means, in real life, not keeping the old "just in case".
**Ride on two horses.** Each has their own road and their own strength, and they ride side by side.

paragraphs: If the old shows itself in a couple as threats or violence, this is no longer a matter for self-reflection: it calls for professional help, and in danger, a local emergency number.

ul: **12, The Hanged Man — entry to the task.** The couple's shared language is pause and pity: "not now", "let it hang for a while", "let's not go there". There is a great deal of tenderness in it. And behind it there is always a door that both of them walk around.

**7, The Chariot — middle of the task.** The two live the task in motion: moves, sudden leaps, new plans, "let's go, maybe it won't catch us". The couple has speed. It does not yet have a horse of its own.
**13, Death — main task.** Not a break-up but the end of an old form: to finish what stayed alive only because nobody touched it.

intro: A Russian fairy tale wrote this plot down almost to the number. In the forbidden closet of Marya Morevna, the fair princess, "there hung Koshchei the Deathless, fettered by twelve chains". The tale knows nothing of tarot or of the destiny matrix, and the twelve chains are a coincidence. But its three acts run in the same order as the cards of the tail: the hanging one, the chase, the death of the Deathless.

faq.q: Does the 12-7-13 tail mean the couple will break up?
faq.a: No. Death in the couple's main task is the end of an old form, not of the union. In the tale it is Koschei who dies, while Ivan and Marya Morevna ride away together, each on their own horse. The numbers do not predict events.

faq.q: Why does the 12-7-13 tail never appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre of the chart. With a main task of 13, an entry of 12 is impossible with any centre, so this triple occurs only in a couple.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. The numbers 12, 7 and 13 form only the 12-7-13 tail, and it occurs in about one couple in 3,647.

faq.q: A couple has the 12-7-13 tail, but the partners' personal tails are different. Is that possible?
faq.a: No. In every couple with this tail the partners' personal tails are 9-12-3 and 3-13-10. If the calculation shows others, the birth dates are worth checking again.

For the couple this is the main task in its plus: an ending that gathers. After the escapes the two are left with pieces: things unsaid, grudges, two versions of one story. The Water of Death is the last conversation after which no further one is needed; signed papers; an unpacked box; parents who have heard a calm "we have decided for ourselves". The minus of the same point is a Death that one partner imposes: one demands that the other "finally change", or looks in the present partner for the features of a former one.

In the tale both mistakes fit into a single exchange. Marya Morevna reproaches him for disobeying her. Ivan answers: "Remember not the past." Each looks at the other's part. Yet the closet was shared: it took both her locked door and his pity.

Arthur Edward Waite's rider of Death "moves slowly" and "carries no visible weapon". Nobody outruns him. In the tale Koschei dies from the hoof of Ivan's horse, burns on a pyre, and his ashes are scattered to the wind: nobody can hang him up again. **The old ends only when it is brought to an end, not when it is hidden.**

The last line of the tale is the strong version of this tail: "Then Marya Morevna mounted Koshchei's horse and Prince Ivan got on his own." The past is not erased: its strength has become her horse. Beside her rides the second rider, on a horse he raised himself. Two horses side by side are The Chariot in its plus: riding together, each on a road of their own.
If the old shows itself in a couple as threats or violence, this is no longer a matter for self-reflection: it calls for professional help, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

unit.title: Koschei in the locked closet

captions.M: Pity each other and keep the closet shut
captions.N: Run from the old: maybe it won't catch up
captions.D: Bring the old to an end, not hang it up again

unit.meaning: Your task is not to lock the old in a closet or run from it, but to bring it to an end and ride on side by side.
